topic: Why the Galápagos Islands are moving and why the eastern islands are older
title: The Galápagos Islands are moving 🌋🐢
hook: Did you know the Galápagos Islands are moving toward Ecuador?

scenes.narration: Did you know the Galápagos Islands are moving toward Ecuador?
And here's something stranger: the eastern islands are millions of years older than the western ones.
It all starts deep down, at a hotspot in the Earth's mantle.
That plume of magma stays put, but the seafloor doesn't: the Nazca Plate moves about five centimeters every year.
scenes.on_screen_text: The plate moves 5 cm a year

scenes.narration: Every time magma punches through the plate, a volcano is born and grows until it rises out of the water.
But the plate carries it away from the hotspot: the volcano dies out and starts to sink.
Meanwhile, a new island is born over the hotspot, and then another, like on a conveyor belt.
That's why Fernandina, in the west, still has active volcanoes, and San Cristóbal, in the east, is up to four million years old.
And underwater, heading toward Ecuador, there are islands that already sank completely, up to nine million years old.
Each island has its own age, climate and food, so its animals changed in different ways.
That's what Charles Darwin saw in eighteen thirty-five, and it helped him think about evolution.
Next time you see the Galápagos, remember you're looking at a line of volcanoes riding on a conveyor belt.
Send this to someone who dreams of visiting the Galápagos.

description: The Galápagos Islands ride on the Nazca Plate, about 5 cm a year, drifting away from the hotspot that built them. That's why the western islands (Fernandina, Isabela) have active volcanoes while the eastern ones (San Cristóbal, Española) are millions of years older. Under the sea, toward Ecuador, the Carnegie Ridge holds islands that already sank. Original 3D animation; figures are approximate.

sources.title: Christie et al. (1992), Drowned islands downstream from the Galapagos hotspot

claims.statement: The Galápagos lie about 1,000 km from mainland Ecuador and the Nazca Plate carries them east/southeast.
The Nazca Plate moves about 5 cm per year (estimates range ~4–6 cm/yr depending on the reference).
Fernandina and Isabela, in the west, have active volcanoes; eastern islands like San Cristóbal and Española have rocks up to ~4 million years old.
The Carnegie Ridge holds flat-topped seamounts (former islands) up to ~9 million years old.
Darwin visited the Galápagos in 1835 aboard HMS Beagle.
